questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Lorentz factor from a speed
questions.learningObjective: State what the Lorentz factor measures for a given speed.
questions.stem: A field technician asks what the Lorentz factor of a signal travelling at 0.8 times the speed of light actually measures.

options.text: It is the factor by which moving clocks slow and lengths shrink along the direction of travel
It is the factor by which the observer's own clock speeds up relative to a moving sample
options.misconception: confuses the gamma factor with a speeding-up clock

options.text: It is the ratio of the signal's speed to the speed of sound in the surrounding air
options.misconception: treats the factor as a comparison with sound speed

options.text: It is the number of times the signal must be reflected before it reaches the receiver
options.misconception: reads gamma as a count of reflections

questions.explanation: The Lorentz factor multiplies rest quantities to give their observed values, so at 0.8 of light speed it is 1.667. Clocks do not speed up for the observer; lengths contract instead.
questions.hint: Gamma is one over the root of one minus beta squared.

options.misconception: claims the stationary observer's clock runs slow

questions.explanation: Time dilation makes the moving vehicle's clock accumulate less proper time than the ground frame's clock for the same pair of events. The ground interval is therefore the longer of the two.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Length of a moving rod measured from outside
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a moving object appears shortened to outside observers.
questions.stem: A survey team measures a moving marker bar from the valley floor and wants to know why its length looks shorter.

answer.exemplar: The bar is shorter in the valley frame because its length is measured along the direction of motion, the only direction in which Lorentz contraction applies. The valley observers see the bar's rest length multiplied by one over gamma, so a bar with a rest length of 2 metres moving at 0.8 of the speed of light measures about 1.2 metres from outside, while the crew riding it still measures 2 metres.

questions.explanation: Length contraction applies only along the direction of motion, so the valley observers see a shorter bar. Transverse dimensions are unchanged, and the crew sees the bar's full rest length.
questions.hint: Only the dimension along the motion appears shortened.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the relativistic momentum of a fast particle.
questions.stem: A cosmic ray tracker in the survey measures a proton moving at 0.8 times the speed of light and asks for its momentum in MeV per c.
questions.explanation: The relativistic momentum is the square root of gamma squared minus one times the rest energy, with gamma of 1.667 here. That gives about 1251 MeV per c for a proton.

answer.exemplar: Each team computes the factor from the same speed measured against the same light speed, so the result must be identical, because the Lorentz factor depends only on the ratio of the measured speed to the speed of light. questions.explanation: The Lorentz factor depends only on the ratio of speed to light speed, so identical speed data gives identical values anywhere. It is a property of the motion, not of the observer or location.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Compton wavelength of the electron
questions.learningObjective: Explain why raising energy does not shrink the Compton wavelength.
questions.stem: A student asks the survey team why the electron Compton wavelength cannot be made smaller by raising the particle's energy.

answer.exemplar: The Compton wavelength depends only on the mass of the scattering particle, fixed by the constants h and the speed of light, so raising the particle energy leaves it unchanged. A higher energy changes the de Broglie wavelength of the particle, which shortens with momentum, but the Compton wavelength stays at 2.43 picometres for the electron, marking the scale where quantum effects in scattering become unavoidable.

questions.explanation: The Compton wavelength depends only on the particle mass and the constants, so energy changes cannot shrink it. The quantity that shrinks with energy is the de Broglie wavelength, a different thing.
questions.hint: It depends on mass, not on the particle's energy.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Total energy of a relativistic electron
questions.learningObjective: Explain why relativistic kinetic energy outgrows the classical formula.
questions.stem: A beam operator asks why the kinetic energy of a fast electron grows much faster than the classical prediction.

answer.exemplar: The kinetic energy is the total energy minus the rest energy, and the total energy carries the gamma factor, which climbs without bound as the speed approaches the speed of light. The classical formula, one half m v squared, only matches the relativistic result at speeds that are tiny compared with the speed of light, so an electron at 0.9 of light speed carries far more kinetic energy than the classical estimate suggests.

questions.explanation: Kinetic energy equals gamma times the rest energy minus the rest energy, and gamma rises steeply with speed. The classical one half m v squared agrees only at speeds far below light speed.
questions.hint: Kinetic energy is total energy minus the rest energy.

answer.exemplar: The Compton wavelength is the length scale at which the quantum nature of the electron becomes unavoidable, set by the electron mass and the constants, about 2.43 picometres for the electron.
